source.title: Widening the Network Mitigates the Impact of Data Heterogeneity on FedAvg

record.file_problem: Text contains the paper through the appendices; some tables/figures are represented in flattened or figure-only form, but the document is not visibly cut off.
record.tranche_reason: Tests how network width affects the FedAvg generalization impact of non-IID client data across MNIST and CIFAR-10 settings, a new federated-learning setting for width and generalization.
record.gate_note: Reports test-accuracy comparisons across widths and IID/non-IID data (Figure 1), and an additional large-width comparison (Figure 2). It also reports parameter and NTK variation and centralized-versus-federated training/test loss, but these do not measure the gap between training and test error named by the claim versions. Theoretical statements are recorded in excerpts, not as empirical rows.
record.test_reason: The study measures how width changes the IID/non-IID performance difference in FedAvg and compares wide FedAvg with centralized GD. It does not establish whether widening beyond the width needed for zero training error keeps lowering test error (V2), or test any other listed version. Its introductory discussion cites overparameterization and implicit regularization as motivation.
record.authors_conclusion: The record captures the authors' conclusion, but needs its theoretical qualifications: under their NTK assumptions and width-scaled learning rate, the model-divergence bound decreases as O(n^(-1/2)). Their infinite-width equivalence with centralized GD additionally uses gradient-flow approximation, shared initialization, matched iterations, and sufficiently small η0τ to neglect higher-order terms. Experiments provide finite-width evidence consistent with these conclusions.
record.recipe_differences: Studies FedAvg on non-IID federated client data, comparing IID and non-IID test accuracy across widths; it does not test the centralized natural-label memorization/generalization setup in the claim versions.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported IID/non-IID test-accuracy difference changes with width and architecture. With η=η0/n, the large-width FNN32 and CNN32 differences are described as nearly absent; narrow FNN1 and CNN1 retain a noticeable gap.

fits_no_version.finding: The reported IID/non-IID accuracy penalty decreases with width within each tested architecture family.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Widening FedAvg models can reduce the held-out accuracy penalty caused by heterogeneous client partitions.

fits_no_version.finding: With learning rate inversely scaled with width, FNN32 has nearly identical IID/non-IID convergence and final accuracy; CNN32 shows a similar trend.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Sufficiently wide FedAvg models with width-scaled learning rates can nearly eliminate IID/non-IID performance differences.

fits_no_version.finding: Section 6.3 and Figure 5 report nearly identical training and testing losses for wide FedAvg and centralized GD under matched iteration counts.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Wide FedAvg can approximate centralized GD's held-out performance under matched initialization and training iterations.

record.peer_reviewed: International Conference on Machine Learning; Proceedings of the 42nd International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 267, 2025
record.problems: Reported quantitative changes in Section 6.1 are relative test-accuracy decreases; exact test-accuracy values are not stated in the text. Large-width comparisons are mainly described from figures and use learning-rate scaling. The experiments concern client-data heterogeneity rather than training-to-test generalization gaps.
record.rows_left_out: No results meeting the row criteria for V1–V8 were reported. The paper also reports NTK and parameter variation in Figure 3, linear-approximation differences in Figure 4, and FedAvg versus centralized training/testing loss in Figure 5; these do not measure a claim-version outcome and are not included as rows.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and its held-out accuracy compared with natural-label training.

Test-error changes beyond an established zero-training-error width. Neither an interpolation threshold nor convergence to zero training error across the empirical width sweep is established; Figure 1 also uses weight decay.
Matched convolutional versus fully connected image-classification comparisons and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive versus SGD optimizer generalization under specified tuning budgets.
Batch-size effects under fixed epoch budgets and adaptations that recover performance.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its ranking of training-to-test generalization gaps.
Retraining after removing memorized versus random examples.

record.verdict_notes: A training-to-test gap is not required for every version: V2 concerns held-out error across widths. The decisive mismatch here is the heterogeneity comparison without an established post-interpolation width regime. Results omitted from the record are already declared in rows_left_out and do not test V1–V8.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization compared with natural-label generalization is not tested.
The paper varies width in FedAvg but does not test one-hidden-layer ReLU networks on MNIST/downsampled CIFAR-10 trained to zero training error or report test error across the interpolation threshold.
Although it evaluates FNNs, CNNs and ResNets, it does not compare convolutional and fully connected networks on the same image task to test the stated architectural advantage.
The paper does not compare adaptive optimizers with SGD for held-out performance.
The paper does not vary batch size or test large-batch penalties under fixed epoch budgets.
The paper does not test dropout.
The paper does not measure magnitude-aware sharpness or compare it with generalization gaps.
The paper does not remove memorized examples or measure the resulting test-accuracy change.
